cues: Imagine the largest ocean on Earth. Now draw a triangle on it. One corner is Hawaii, one corner is Aotearoa, New Zealand, one corner is Rapa Nui, Easter Island.
Inside that triangle lie about 10 million square miles of open water, more than twice the size of the United States and more than a thousand islands scattered across it like seeds.
Imagine, every one of those islands was found and settled by people in voyaging canoes. No compass, no charts, no metal. They began about 3,000 years ago, reaching Tonga and Samoa.
Then generation after generation, they pushed east and north and south unto the unknown.
The last great wave, 700 to 800 years ago, reached the farthest corners, Hawaii, Rapa Nui, and Aotearoa, among the last places on Earth that human beings ever reached.
Why did they go to find new land for their children? And they did not drift there.
They went on purpose, reading the stars, the swells, the birds, and the clouds, and they carried their families, their plants, and their animals with them.
By the 20th century, many experts believed the Pacific had been settled by accident, by canoes blown off course and people washing ashore.
So, in 1976, a voyaging canoe called Hōkūleʻa, about 60 feet long with two hulls and woven sails left Maui for Tahiti, 2,500 miles of open ocean.
The man guiding it was Mau Piailug from Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia.
His grandfather chose him when he was about five years old.
As a small boy, he was set in the warm tide pools, so the ocean would never frighten him.
At 18, he was initiated as a navigator.
He was one of the very few people left on Earth who still carried this knowledge whole.
How do you cross 2,500 miles with nothing?
Mau's tradition divides the horizon into houses, the places where the stars rise and set.
A star is only useful for steering while it is low, for about an hour and a half.
Then it climbs too high, and the navigator moves to the next star, rising in the same house.
The star changes all night, the direction does not.
And in the dark, he lay in the hull and felt the long ocean swells with his whole body.
And calm came first, a navigator who panics cannot read the ocean.
After 31 days, they sighted land, the Atoll of Mataiva.
Three days later, they sailed into Tahiti, and more than 17,000 were waiting at the harbor.
The question was answered.
Our ancestors crossed the greatest ocean on Earth because they could read it.
Then Mau did something even more remarkable.
Instead of keeping what he knew, he gave it away.
He spent 28 months teaching a young Hawaiian,
Nainoa Thompson, so it would not die with him.
In 2007, on Satawal, he raised 16 new navigators, five of them Hawaiian.
Because one man chose to hand it on, canoes cross the Pacific by the stars again.
And Hōkūleʻa has sailed around the world.
Our lives, your life, is the same.
Plans, markets, and people move all the time like the stars.
What is your house?
The one direction that holds when everything else moves.
This week, write it down in one short phrase.
One night, step outside.
Find a star low on the horizon.
And watch it rise.
Before each hard decision, check it against your phrase.
